Chapter three. The replay.

Here's the setup. Ten thousand euros into world stocks, on the last day of 1999. Right at the top.

M S C I World, dividends reinvested, measured in euros, after a zero point two percent yearly fee. No cherry picking.

Question two. By the end of 2002, how much of your ten thousand euros was left?

Eight thousand nine hundred, seven thousand two hundred, or five thousand five hundred? Five thousand five hundred.

Forty-five percent gone in three years. And remember, this is the whole world index. Not a tech fund.

Then the recovery starts. 2003, 2004, 2005. By the end of 2006, you're at eight thousand seven hundred. Almost there.

And then, 2008.

By the end of 2008, your portfolio is worth five thousand three hundred euros.

Read that again. Nine years in, you have less money than at the bottom of the dot-com crash.

So when are you finally back above ten thousand euros?

In 2013.

Thirteen years. Thirteen years of doing everything right, and having nothing to show for it.

If you started investing in your thirties, you'd be close to fifty before you saw a profit.

And it wasn't a quiet thirteen years. You lived through two crashes of almost fifty percent each. Your bank advisor, the news, your friends, everyone told you stocks were dead.

By the way, if you saw my short on this, the start date there was January 2001, and the answer was twelve years. Starting at the very top makes it one year worse.

Now, the other side of the story. That same ten thousand euros, invested at the worst possible moment, is worth about forty-six thousand euros today.

That's about five point nine percent a year, for almost twenty-seven years. After the dot-com crash, after 2008, after Covid, after 2022.

And before you say, yes, but inflation: prices in the euro area rose about seventy-six percent from 1999 to 2025. So in today's money, your ten thousand euros became roughly two and a half times as much. Still a real gain.

And the crashes kept coming. In 2020, Covid sent markets down by a third in a few weeks. In 2022, world stocks lost almost thirteen percent in euros, while bonds fell too.

Each one felt like the end of the world at the time. On this chart, they're small dents.

So buying at the top did not ruin you. Selling at the bottom would have.

But most of you don't invest a lump sum on one day. You invest every month. So let's replay that too.

Three hundred euros a month, starting in January 2000. Straight into the crash.

End of 2002. You've put in ten thousand eight hundred euros. It's worth seven thousand two hundred.

End of 2008, after nine years of saving: thirty-two thousand four hundred in, twenty-three thousand four hundred left. That's the moment most people quit.

But those were the months when every three hundred euros bought the most shares. The crash years were your best buying years.

Today, you've put in ninety-six thousand euros. The plan is worth about four hundred and sixteen thousand.

The crash didn't hurt the monthly saver. It paid them. But only if they kept going.
